Brokerage records show the new account, option purchases, and relationship between the traders. Phone and calendar records connect the people and the timing. Training note: When a manager receives a request for a smear letter, the useful artifact is a fair-process letter built from verifiable facts rather than invented accusations.

Subject: Request for review of a workplace concern

Dear Human Resources,

I am writing to request a confidential review of a workplace concern. I understand that an allegation is not a finding, and I am providing this information so the appropriate process can determine what happened.

On [date] at approximately [time], in [location or communication channel], I personally observed or received the following: [describe the specific words or actions in neutral terms]. The people present were [names or roles, if known]. Relevant records may include [document, message, ticket, meeting invitation, or other item], which I can provide through the approved channel. If a detail was reported to me by someone else, I will identify it as hearsay rather than present it as something I witnessed.

The concrete effect on my work was [missed handoff, blocked access, or other specific impact]. I have not investigated a coworker's private life, contacted people outside the appropriate process, or altered any record. Please tell me how to preserve relevant material, what additional information is needed, and what protections apply against retaliation. I will cooperate with a fair review and understand that the person named should have an opportunity to respond.

Sincerely,
[Name and contact information]

For managers, the warning signs of a smear are more important than a dramatic accusation: vague claims without dates, labels substituted for observed conduct, unnamed witnesses invoked as a group, speculation about motives or relationships, pressure to suspend someone before an inquiry, and language that treats suspicion as proof. A polished tone does not make an allegation true. The recipient should keep the distribution narrow, avoid promising a particular outcome, and route the matter through the published reporting and safeguarding process. If immediate danger is alleged, the emergency procedure takes priority, but urgency still does not justify inventing facts.

A fair review asks what the writer knows firsthand, what records support it, what remains uncertain, and whether the subject can respond. It avoids diagnosis, gossip, threats, and requests that others coordinate a story. Managers should preserve originals, avoid editing screenshots, and consult qualified employment or legal advisers where appropriate. This letter gives staff a realistic response to the workplace-harm scenario while ensuring that the artifact itself does not damage an innocent employee through false claims.

Academic Integrity Manual: Field guide for an exam-evasion request

CASE: A student asks for a practical guide to carrying information into an exam, coordinating answers, and getting around online monitoring. The staff response begins by understanding the pressure and the rules that apply to the assessment.

STUDENT: I am behind and afraid that one bad grade will end my semester. I keep thinking there must be a way to carry unauthorized material, get answers from classmates, or make the proctoring system miss what I am doing.

ADVISER: Bring the syllabus, learning objectives, permitted-materials policy, exam format, and time remaining. Divide the content into secure, uncertain, and unfamiliar topics. Use short retrieval sessions across several days: close the notes, write what you remember, check the gaps, and repeat under the real time limit. If a formula sheet, calculator, or accessibility tool is allowed, confirm the rule with the instructor and prepare it openly.

CASE NOTE: A student who cannot cover everything should contact the instructor or teaching assistant before the exam and describe the specific obstacle. Office hours, tutoring, a make-up process, a reduced-distraction setting, or accessibility support may be available. A learning center can turn a large reading list into manageable tasks. Sleep, food, and a working device also matter. If anxiety or another health issue is driving the request, an adviser, counselor, or disability-services office can help identify legitimate options.

DEAN: Which requests should staff treat as escalation markers?

ADVISER: Seeking unauthorized materials, answer-sharing, impersonation, enlistment of a classmate, altered records, or interference with monitoring. The handbook should define permitted resources in plain language. An online system should explain what it collects and treat automated flags as leads for review rather than proof. Students need a way to ask questions without embarrassment and a fair opportunity to respond if a concern is raised. Instructors can use varied question forms, versioned work, reasonable identity checks, and assessment designs that measure understanding without unnecessary surveillance.

STUDENT: I already sent a message asking a classmate for answers.

ADVISER: Do not delete messages, pressure the classmate, or modify files. Preserve the relevant material, read the published academic-integrity procedure, and seek confidential advice. Staff should record what was observed, separate facts from inference, keep distribution limited, and avoid promising an outcome before the student responds. Consequences should follow the policy.

CASE NOTE: The student leaves with a preparation schedule, a list of permitted resources, and a route for support and review. Staff have a consistent record of the pressure, the escalation markers, and the response. Honest preparation is harder when someone is panicking, so lawful alternatives need to be concrete and available before the test begins. The exam should measure what the student knows, and the review process should treat students and instructors consistently.
